analysis.one_liner: Sets a Medicaid hospital payment floor at 90% of Medicare rates and bars cuts to medically necessary inpatient care.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after its introduction it sat in a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee until the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required states to pay hospitals at least 90% of what Medicare pays for inpatient care for Medicaid patients, adjusted for how sick the patients are. It would also have barred states from putting limits on the amount, duration, or scope of Medicaid coverage for medically necessary hospital stays, and required an extra payment adjustment for unusually costly or long stays so hospitals would not lose money on the sickest patients. The changes were set to take effect January 1, 1991, and states could not have gotten waivers around them.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicaid beneficiaries would gain guaranteed access to medically necessary inpatient hospital care, since states could no longer cap covered hospital services. Hospitals that treat large numbers of Medicaid patients, especially those serving low-income and disabled populations, would gain from higher payment rates closer to Medicare levels.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicaid patients and hospitals serving them

how_it_helps.text: Medicaid payments for inpatient hospital services would have to be at least 90% of what Medicare would pay for the same services, adjusted for case mix, patient age and disability, and other factors, effective January 1, 1991 [S3].

State Medicaid plans could not impose any limitation on the amount, duration, or scope of coverage for medically necessary inpatient hospital services, which would prevent states from capping hospital benefits for enrollees [S2] [S3].

States using prospective payment would have to include outlier adjustments for exceptionally costly cases or unusually long stays, so hospitals would not be underpaid for treating the sickest Medicaid patients [S2] [S3].

The Secretary of Health and Human Services would review and approve or disapprove each state's plan amendment, and could not waive the new requirements under section 1115 or 1915(b) demonstrations [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State governments and the federal Medicaid program would bear higher payment costs, since raising the payment floor to 90% of Medicare rates increases total spending on inpatient hospital services. Hospitals and states paid below that floor would see their budgets rise.
analysis.who_pays_short: State Medicaid budgets and the federal government

drawbacks.text: Raising the payment floor to 90% of Medicare rates would substantially increase Medicaid spending for states below that level, and states would either raise taxes, cut other services, or reduce other Medicaid payments to absorb the cost [S3].

Barring states from limiting the amount, duration, or scope of medically necessary inpatient coverage would remove a cost-control tool states use to manage Medicaid budgets, which some states argued was needed to keep the program solvent [S2].
The payment floor and outlier requirements could not be waived even through demonstration waivers, reducing state flexibility to test alternative delivery and payment arrangements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: Medicaid patients in states with very low hospital payment rates or hard caps on covered hospital days would get stronger access to care, and hospitals that treat them would be less undercompensated. The cost is also real: the mandate falls on state budgets, which would have to find the money, and the bill gives states no flexibility through waivers. It is a straightforward pro-provider, pro-beneficiary mandate whose main question is who pays — and the answer is mostly state and federal taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health and the Environment Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Pete Stark introduced the bill on January 31, 1989, with no cosponsors [S1] [S4].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on February 13, 1989 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action, and the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State Medicaid budgets benefited, since they never had to raise hospital payments to the Medicare-linked floor or remove caps on covered hospital care. Hospitals and Medicaid patients in low-paying states gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: State Medicaid budgets; hospitals and patients gained nothing

for.name: Rep. Fortney Pete Stark
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to set a Medicaid hospital payment floor and bar limits on medically necessary inpatient coverage; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never reported it out; it was passed to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment and no hearing or markup followed.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and the Environment
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from February 13, 1989 until the Congress ended without taking it up.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no party split is recorded; it had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party [S4].

industries.industry: Hospitals (especially those treating large Medicaid caseloads)
industries.note: The bill would have raised Medicaid inpatient payments to at least 90% of Medicare rates and required outlier payments for the costliest cases, directly increasing hospital revenue. Better payment also reduces the risk that hospitals turn away or skimp on Medicaid patients, so the industry's interest here runs alongside patients'.

States would have had to pay more for inpatient hospital care and give up the ability to cap covered hospital services or waive the requirements. The added cost funds care for Medicaid enrollees, but it comes out of state budgets that also finance schools and other services.
